(CNN)  -- Over 28,000 Liverpool fans marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster in a special memorial service at Anfield on Wednesday. Liverpool supporters at the Kop end paid their respects in an emotional afternoon at Anfield. A total of 96 supporters died on April 15, 1989 before the FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium, the worst-ever tragedy in English sporting history. To commemorate the anniversary, the city of Liverpool came to a standstill at 3.06 pm (1406 GMT) with the bells of the two cathedrals and its civic buildings ringing out in memory of those fans who lost their lives. On Anfield's famous Kop, 96 candles were lit while commemorations took place at Hillsborough and also in Nottingham. Members of the current Liverpool team stood somberly as hymns were played before a roll call of the dead was read out. Club legend Kenny Dalglish, who was Liverpool manager at the time of the disaster, then read a short prayer. The mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotherham, who was at the game 20 years ago, helped organize the emotional memorial. "Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK," he said. "I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, whose 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim of the tragedy, spoke of his feelings this week. "Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget. So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them." The Liverpool fans died in a crush which started just before the kick-off as the gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened with terrible consequences. The match started but when the scale of the tragedy became clear, it was swiftly abandoned at 3.06 pm. In the immediate aftermath, the British government commissioned Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry which would have a far-reaching impact on football. Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

LIVERPOOL, England — Families, survivors, and supporters gathered this week to mark another anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster, the crush that killed 97 Liverpool football fans in April 1989, in a memorial service that organizers say continues to honor victims while pressing for what they call unfinished justice.

## The Disaster

The tragedy unfolded on April 15, 1989, at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, England, during an FA Cup semi-final match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. As thousands of Liverpool supporters attempted to enter the stadium's Leppings Lane terrace, overcrowding led to a fatal human crush. Ninety-seven people ultimately died as a result of injuries sustained that day, making it the deadliest disaster in British sporting history.

In the disaster's immediate aftermath, police and some media outlets wrongly blamed drunken and unruly fans for causing the crush — a narrative that would haunt survivors and victims' families for decades and delay their pursuit of justice.

## The Taylor Report

Lord Justice Peter Taylor was appointed to lead an official inquiry into the disaster, and his findings, published in stages during 1989 and 1990, proved damning for authorities. The Taylor Report concluded that the primary cause of the disaster was a failure of police control, directly contradicting early claims that fan behavior was to blame.

The report led to sweeping changes in English football, most notably the mandate that top-division stadiums convert to all-seater venues, eliminating the standing terraces where the crush occurred. The Taylor Report is widely credited with reshaping stadium safety standards across the United Kingdom and influencing similar reforms internationally.

Despite the report's clear findings, it would take decades — including a 2016 inquest that formally ruled the victims were unlawfully killed — before institutional acknowledgment of police failures was fully realized.

## Reactions and Renewed Calls for Justice

At this year's memorial, family members reiterated calls for a "Hillsborough Law" — legislation that would impose a legal duty of candor on public officials and institutions, aimed at preventing the kind of cover-ups and institutional defensiveness that marked the disaster's aftermath.

Politicians attending or issuing statements around the anniversary echoed themes of remembrance and reform. Members of Parliament representing Liverpool constituencies have continued to push the government to fully implement proposed accountability legislation, arguing that meaningful change requires binding legal obligations rather than symbolic gestures.

"The families have waited over three decades for truth," said one local MP in remarks to reporters. "Words of sympathy are not enough. We need the law changed so no other community has to fight this hard for justice."

Fan groups, including the Hillsborough Family Support Group and supporters' unions from clubs across England, used the anniversary to renew pressure on lawmakers, framing the push for a Hillsborough Law as a legacy issue that extends far beyond football.

Liverpool Football Club also marked the occasion with tributes at Anfield, continuing a tradition of remembrance that has become deeply embedded in the club's identity, with the phrase "You'll Never Walk Alone" serving as both anthem and rallying cry for justice campaigns tied to the disaster.

## Looking Ahead

While the Taylor Report fundamentally transformed stadium safety in British football, campaigners insist the broader lessons about institutional accountability remain incompletely realized. As the anniversary events concluded, family members and supporters vowed to continue advocating for legislative change, insisting that the memory of the 97 victims demands more than commemoration — it demands systemic reform.
